subtopics.title: US Military Strike and Justifications
subtopics.summary: United States forces carried out a military strike on Venezuela, known as Operation Absolute Resolve, which led to the capture of President Nicolas Maduro. Washington cited illegal migration, narcotics trafficking and alleged narco-terrorism, claims that Venezuela strongly contests. The action raised the question of whether a law enforcement objective can justify the use of military force on a sovereign territory.
facts: Operation Absolute Resolve: US military strike on Venezuela
Strike locations named: Caracas, Miranda, Aragua and La Guaira
The strike led to the capture of President Nicolas Maduro
US justifications: illegal migration, narcotics trafficking, alleged narco-terrorism
Venezuela rejects these claims and calls them a pretext for regime change
Washington designated Tren de Aragua and Cartel de los Soles as Foreign Terrorist Organisations
US alleges Cartel de los Soles operates under the leadership of Maduro
US alleges Cartel of the Suns collaborated with FARC to traffic cocaine into the US
Arguments in favour: fentanyl and narco-gangs cause mass American deaths
Arguments against: crime can become an excuse to violate borders

subtopics.title: Venezuela's Political and Economic Crisis
subtopics.summary: Venezuela has faced a deep political and economic collapse for several years, marked by hyperinflation, power outages, food shortages and a breakdown of healthcare services. The crisis escalated when Juan Guaido, Head of the National Assembly, declared himself Acting President, challenging Maduro's second term that began in January 2019. Nearly 8 million Venezuelans have fled the country since 2013, mainly to Latin American countries.
facts: Hyperinflation, prolonged power outages and food shortages cause severe humanitarian distress
Breakdown of healthcare services is part of the humanitarian crisis
Guaido declared himself Acting President, citing Articles 233 and 333 of the Venezuelan Constitution
Maduro was sworn in for a controversial second term in January 2019
The 2018 presidential elections were widely criticised as unfair and non-transparent
Opposition leaders were barred, imprisoned or exiled
The opposition-controlled National Assembly called Maduro a 'Usurper'
Economic contraction under Maduro is largely blamed on corruption, poor governance and overdependence on oil
Nearly 8 million Venezuelans have fled since 2013, mainly to Latin American countries
Currency: Venezuelan Bolivar; official language: Spanish

subtopics.title: US Sanctions and Strategic Interests
subtopics.summary: Washington imposed comprehensive sanctions on PDVSA, Venezuela's state-owned oil firm, to cut Maduro's access to oil revenue. Because sanctions failed to dislodge the government, the US turned to maritime interdictions aimed at choking oil revenues. Strategic interests include Venezuela's very large oil reserves and its partnerships with China, Russia, Iran and Cuba.
facts: US imposed comprehensive sanctions targeting PDVSA, the state-owned oil firm
Sanctions drastically limited Venezuela's oil exports to the US, forcing Caracas to seek alternative buyers
Maduro severed diplomatic ties with the US and expelled American diplomats
Venezuela has the world's largest proven crude oil reserves, estimated at over 300 billion barrels
Sanctions failed to dislodge the Maduro government, so the US turned to maritime interdictions
Venezuela's partnerships with China, Russia, Iran and Cuba cover energy, defence and finance
US views these alignments as a challenge to its strategic dominance in the Western Hemisphere
US revived Monroe Doctrine rhetoric, termed the 'Don-roe Doctrine'
Caribbean is treated as a critical zone of influence, reminiscent of Cold War-era calculations

subtopics.title: Monroe Doctrine and Limits of Multilateralism
subtopics.summary: The Monroe Doctrine, proclaimed in 1823, was initially defensive but later became a basis for US intervention in Latin America, expanded through the Roosevelt Corollary of 1904. The UN struggles to prevent unilateral interventions because of Security Council vetoes, unpaid dues and gray-zone tactics. Reform proposals include limiting P5 veto use and creating an accountability protocol for gray-zone threats.
facts: Monroe Doctrine: unilateral US foreign policy declaration proclaimed in 1823 by President James Monroe
Originally aimed to stop European powers from re-colonising Latin America
Roosevelt Corollary (1904) justified US intervention to maintain stability in the Western Hemisphere
Three core principles: non-colonisation, non-intervention, and US non-interference in Europe
P5 members (US, Russia, China, UK, France) can block any UN Security Council resolution
47 vetoes blocked 37 draft resolutions between 2015 and 2024
UN faces $2.4B in unpaid regular dues and a $2.7B peacekeeping shortfall
NATO, AU and ECOWAS intervene without UNSC approval
Modern gray-zone conflicts use cyberattacks, PMCs and proxies
Reform ideas: limit P5 veto use and introduce a veto override for mass atrocities

subtopics.title: Greenland's Status within Denmark, NATO and the EU
subtopics.summary: Greenland is one of Denmark's two autonomous territories and became a Danish colony after Hans Egede's expedition arrived in 1721. It became a self-governing territory in 1979 and has held the right to declare independence through a referendum since 2009. Through Denmark it is part of NATO, while it is associated with the EU as one of the EU Overseas Countries and Territories.
facts: Greenland is the world's largest island and one of Denmark's two autonomous territories
The other autonomous territory of Denmark is the Faroe Islands
Greenland became a Danish colony in the early 18th century after Hans Egede's expedition arrived in 1721
Greenland became a self-governing territory in 1979
Since 2009 Greenland has had the right to declare independence through a referendum
Greenland is part of NATO by default because Denmark is a NATO member
Greenland is not an EU member state but is associated with the EU as an Overseas Country and Territory
Greenlanders are considered to be EU citizens
Greenland joined the European Community with Denmark in 1973 and left it in 1985

subtopics.title: US Strategic and Military Ties with Greenland
subtopics.summary: The United States seized temporary control of Greenland during the Second World War to stop Nazi Germany from exploiting the Danish colony. It proposed a $100 million purchase offer to Denmark in 1946 and formalised American military access through a 1951 defence agreement. Today the US maintains Pituffik Space Base, which helps monitor potential missile threats.
facts: The US seized temporary control of Greenland in World War II
The aim was to prevent Nazi Germany from exploiting the Danish colony after Denmark's occupation
In 1946 the US proposed a $100 million offer to Denmark for outright purchase of Greenland
The 1951 US-Denmark Defence Agreement formalised American military access to Greenland
Pituffik Space Base, formerly known as Thule Air Base, is maintained by the US
The base monitors potential missile threats from Russia, China and North Korea
Greenland hosts critical infrastructure for the US Ballistic Missile Early-Warning System
Greenland lies within the GIUK Gap, a key chokepoint for monitoring naval movements in the North Atlantic
Greenland's ground stations can track polar-orbiting satellites
Greenland enhances NATO's ability to monitor Russian activities in the Arctic and North Atlantic

subtopics.title: Critical Minerals and Emerging Arctic Shipping Routes
subtopics.summary: Greenland has large untapped reserves of rare earth elements, which are crucial for semiconductors, renewable energy and defence systems. These reserves offer the West an alternative supply chain to China-dominated rare earth markets. Melting Arctic ice is opening new maritime corridors, such as the Transpolar Sea Route, that could shorten Atlantic-Pacific travel and bypass the Panama and Suez Canals.
facts: Greenland possesses large untapped reserves of rare earth elements
Rare earth elements are crucial for semiconductors, renewable energy technologies and defence systems
China dominates the rare earth elements market
Greenland offers the West an alternative supply chain to China-dominated rare earth markets
Melting Arctic ice is opening new maritime corridors
The Transpolar Sea Route is one of the emerging Arctic shipping routes
New Arctic routes could reduce travel time between the Atlantic and Pacific Oceans
New Arctic routes could lower fuel and shipping costs
New Arctic routes could bypass the Panama Canal and Suez Canal
Control over Arctic sea lanes will shape future global trade and naval power projection

subtopics.title: Great Power Competition and the EU Anti-Coercion Instrument
subtopics.summary: China labels itself a Near-Arctic State and invests in Arctic research, while Russia has heavily militarised its Arctic coastline and the US views Greenland as central to countering both. Denmark's firm stance highlights the tension between territorial sovereignty and the strategic ambitions of major powers. The EU's Anti-Coercion Instrument, nicknamed the Trade Bazooka, is primarily a deterrent tool against economic coercion.
facts: China labels itself a 'Near-Arctic State'
China is investing in Arctic research and infrastructure
Russia has heavily militarised its Arctic coastline
The US views Greenland as central to countering both China and Russia
Denmark takes a firm stance on sovereignty over Greenland
The EU's Anti-Coercion Instrument is nicknamed the 'Trade Bazooka'
The Anti-Coercion Instrument is primarily a deterrent tool with capacity for proportionate retaliation
The Anti-Coercion Instrument responds when a non-EU country seeks to coerce the EU through trade or investment measures
Its objectives are to deter economic coercion and protect the EU's strategic autonomy
A French President urged the EU to invoke the Anti-Coercion Instrument for the first time against US tariffs amid the Greenland dispute

subtopics.title: Charter, Mandate and Leadership
subtopics.summary: The US is constituting a Board of Peace, a US-led inter-governmental body established under UN Security Council Resolution 2803 (2025) and linked to the 20-point Gaza peace plan. Its charter has 13 Articles, and its chair is the US President. The Board's mandate covers supervising Gaza's civil and security bodies, mobilising assistance and ensuring accountability during Gaza's transition.
facts: Type: US-led inter-governmental body
Established under UN Security Council Resolution 2803 (2025)
Charter contains 13 Articles on membership, financial contributions and dispute redressal
Mandate: supervise and guide NCAG (civil administration) and ISF (security)
Mandate: mobilise international financial and technical assistance
Mandate: ensure transparency, coordination and accountability during transition
Chair: US President Donald Trump, who also serves separately as Inaugural Representative of the US
Chair can be removed only if he resigns voluntarily or is unanimously declared incapable by the Executive Board
Executive Board includes former UK PM Tony Blair, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio, World Bank President Ajay Banga and Jared Kushner
US announced the Board meets with 19 countries; India is absent from this high-level initiative

subtopics.title: Membership and Gaza Governance Bodies
subtopics.summary: Membership of the Board requires a country to consent to be bound by its charter, and it is offered on a rotational or a permanent basis. Gaza's civil administration is handled by the National Committee for the Administration of Gaza (NCAG), with Nickolay Mladenov as High Representative linking the Board and the NCAG on the ground. The Gaza Executive Board is a supporting operational body that coordinates on-the-ground activities.
facts: Membership requires a country to consent to be bound by the Charter
Rotational membership: 3-year tenure without mandatory financial contribution
Permanent membership: available through a reported contribution of USD 1 billion
Initial authorisation of the Board lasts until 31 December 2027
High Representative for Gaza: Bulgarian diplomat Nickolay Mladenov, on-the-ground liaison between Board and NCAG
NCAG: 15-member committee of politically independent Palestinian technocrats
NCAG is chaired by Ali Shaath, a former Palestinian Authority Deputy Minister
NCAG is responsible for day-to-day civil administration
Gaza Executive Board: supporting operational body that coordinates on-the-ground activities
Gaza Executive Board members: US, UK, Turkey, Qatar, Egypt, UAE, Cyprus and Netherlands; no Palestinian representative

subtopics.title: Key Features of the US 20-point Gaza Plan
subtopics.summary: The US plan, officially titled the Comprehensive Plan to End the Gaza Conflict, envisions a demilitarised Gaza with an immediate ceasefire and the release of all hostages. It pairs security arrangements, including the International Stabilization Force (ISF), with humanitarian aid and reconstruction through a special economic zone. The plan excludes Hamas from governance while offering amnesty to members who decommission their weapons.
facts: Gaza is envisioned as a demilitarised, terror-free zone
An immediate ceasefire is mandated, halting military actions by both sides
All hostages, alive or deceased, must be released within 72 hours of Israel's formal acceptance
Israel frees 250 Palestinian life-sentence prisoners and 1,700 detainees
Hamas members who decommission weapons get amnesty or safe passage abroad
Full humanitarian aid enters immediately; Rafah crossing reopens under agreement
Special economic zone with favourable trade terms, supported by international investment
No forced displacement: people are free to stay, leave or return
Hamas is excluded from governance; ISF deployed to secure Gaza and train police
Interfaith dialogue platform created to promote religious harmony

subtopics.title: UN Reform and the Board's Significance
subtopics.summary: Reform of the UN system is treated as urgent because ad hoc peacebuilding missions end once crises subside and UN Security Council reform is deadlocked. The booklet presents the Board as an incremental innovation within existing structures, using the General Assembly's power under Article 22 of the UN Charter. The Board is also described as a move from universal multilateral institutions towards leader-centric mini-lateral mechanisms.
facts: UN peacebuilding missions often end once immediate crises subside
Prolonged deadlock over comprehensive UNSC reform has paralysed timely action
Under Article 22 of the UN Charter, the General Assembly can establish subsidiary bodies without Charter amendment
Board of Peace is presented as reform from within, not replacement of the UNSC
Board aims to institutionalise long-term political engagement and prevent relapse into conflict
Represents a move from universal multilateral institutions to mini-lateral, leader-centric mechanisms
Emphasises political authority, resource mobilisation and rapid decision-making over consensus-based diplomacy
Projected as a template for managing complex global conflicts
Signals evolving US thinking on conflict resolution and post-war governance

topics.title: Diego Garcia and the Chagos Islands

subtopics.title: Sovereignty Deal and Diego Garcia Base
subtopics.summary: Britain has agreed to transfer sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius, but the UK will retain sovereign rights over Diego Garcia. A joint UK-US military base there will remain operational for an initial period of 99 years. US concerns centre on strategic autonomy and base security, and Trump criticised the plan.
facts: Britain has agreed to transfer sovereignty of the Chagos Islands to Mauritius.
The Chagos archipelago comprises 58 islands, with Diego Garcia the largest.
The UK retains sovereign rights over Diego Garcia under the agreement.
A joint UK-US military base on Diego Garcia will remain operational for an initial period of 99 years.
Diego Garcia is located in the Central Indian Ocean.
US concern: a sovereignty change may affect strategic autonomy and base security.
Trump criticised the UK plan, citing the strategic importance of the US military base.
The issue is sensitive because it pits decolonisation against security interests.

subtopics.title: Chagos Dispute and Legal Battles
subtopics.summary: The UK declared the Chagos Islands a British Indian Ocean Territory in 1965, and the islands stayed with Britain when Mauritius became independent in 1968. Between 1968 and 1973, native Chagossians were forcibly removed to make way for a military base. Mauritius then pursued legal routes, including a case at the Permanent Court of Arbitration and an ICJ advisory opinion that ended in a 2019 order to return the islands.
facts: The UK declared the Chagos Islands a British Indian Ocean Territory in 1965.
Chagos remained with Britain when Mauritius gained independence in 1968.
Between 1968 and 1973, the UK and US forcibly removed native Chagossians.
In 2015, Mauritius initiated legal proceedings against the UK at the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague.
The Permanent Court of Arbitration ruled that the UK violated Mauritius' rights under UNCLOS.
The Court found that the UK had ulterior motives in creating a Marine Protected Area around the Chagos Islands in 2010.
The UK insisted that the issue should remain a bilateral matter.
In 2017, the UNGA voted on Mauritius' resolution to seek an ICJ advisory opinion.
In 2019, the ICJ ordered the UK to return the Chagos Islands to Mauritius.
The UK claimed that the ICJ had no jurisdiction over the matter.

subtopics.title: Colonial History of the Chagos Islands
subtopics.summary: Portuguese navigators discovered the Chagos Islands in the 16th century, and the islands later came under French control. After Napoleon's defeat, Britain took control of both Chagos and Mauritius, and France ceded the islands to Britain in 1814. Mauritius later argued that it had been coerced into giving up the islands, in violation of UN Resolution 1514.
facts: Portuguese navigators discovered the Chagos Islands in the 16th century.
The Chagos Islands later came under French control.
After Napoleon's defeat, Britain took control of both Chagos and Mauritius.
In 1814, France ceded the islands to Britain.
Mauritius argued that it was coerced into giving up the islands during colonial rule.
UN Resolution 1514 prohibited the breakup of colonies before independence.
The UK claimed that the ICJ had no jurisdiction over the matter.
Mauritius is a former British and French colony that gained independence from British rule in 1968.

subtopics.title: Mauritius and India Partnership
subtopics.summary: India and Mauritius established diplomatic relations in 1948, and the partnership now covers security, trade and culture. Mauritius is a key source of investment into India and a gateway for Indian trade into Africa. India has also supported Mauritius on security and disaster response, including naval drills and an airfield upgrade.
facts: Mauritius is an island nation in the Western Indian Ocean, with its capital at Port Louis.
India and Mauritius established diplomatic relations in 1948.
Mahatma Gandhi visited Mauritius in 1901.
The Indira Gandhi Centre for Indian Culture (1987) is India's largest cultural centre abroad.
The 2021 CECPA was the first such agreement between India and an African nation.
Bilateral trade in FY 2024-25 was USD 887.25 million.
Mauritius was the second largest source of FDI into India in FY 2024-25, after Singapore.
India was the first responder for Mauritius during COVID-19, the Wakashio oil spill (2020) and Cyclone Chido.
Mauritius participates in India-led VARUNA and MILAN naval drills.
India upgraded the Agaléga Island airstrip into a full-length airfield.

subtopics.title: MAHASAGAR and Maritime Initiatives
subtopics.summary: MAHASAGAR is an Indian Navy initiative launched in 2023 that builds on India's 2015 SAGAR maritime doctrine. It widens the focus from India's immediate neighbourhood to the broader Global South, with trade, security, technology and finance as key areas. New tools under it include the IOS Sagar platform and the AIKEYME naval exercise with African nations.
facts: MAHASAGAR builds on India's 2015 Maritime Doctrine, SAGAR.
MAHASAGAR was launched by the Indian Navy in 2023.
MAHASAGAR widens the scope of SAGAR from India's immediate maritime neighbourhood to the broader Global South.
MAHASAGAR's key focus areas are trade for development, mutual security, technology sharing and financial assistance.
MAHASAGAR is a bi-annual initiative that convenes naval chiefs and maritime officials from littoral states.
IOS Sagar uses the INS Sunayna platform to deepen naval cooperation with Indian Ocean littorals.
AIKEYME is a large-scale naval exercise with African nations.
AIKEYME means Unity in Sanskrit, symbolising solidarity with African partners.

subtopics.title: Mukalla Port airstrike and STC standoff
subtopics.summary: Saudi Arabia struck Mukalla Port and UAE-backed STC units after alleging an arms shipment for separatists, which Abu Dhabi denied. The STC refused Riyadh's call to withdraw from contested areas, and the UAE pulled its troops out of Saudi Arabia. The episode shows divisions within the anti-Houthi coalition despite shared opposition to the Houthis.
facts: Saudi Arabia carried out airstrikes on Mukalla Port in southern Yemen.
The strike followed the arrival of a consignment from Fujairah (UAE).
Riyadh alleged the consignment contained arms meant for southern separatist groups.
Abu Dhabi said the shipment consisted of vehicles meant exclusively for UAE forces.
Saudi aircraft also struck UAE-supported STC units, with strikes reported in Hadramout.
Saudi-aligned National Shield Forces sought to take over STC military installations.
Riyadh called for STC fighters to withdraw from contested areas; the STC refused.
Saudi Arabia asked the UAE to withdraw its military elements within 24 hours.
UAE cited escalating airstrikes as a security risk to its personnel.

subtopics.title: Yemen's North-South divide and Houthi insurgency
subtopics.summary: North and South Yemen were separate states until their 1990 merger, and centralised power after unification fuelled southern resentment. A secession attempt in 1994 and the Southern Movement formed in 2007 reflect this divide. The Houthi insurgency began in 2004, and the Houthis captured Sanaa in 2014.
facts: North and South Yemen differed in religious traditions, social structures and governance systems.
Until 1990, Yemen existed as two states: the Yemeni Arab Republic (North) and the PDRY (South).
The North was supported by the United States and Saudi Arabia; the South was backed by the Soviet Union.
In 1990 the two states merged to form the Republic of Yemen under Ali Abdullah Saleh.
Southern leaders attempted secession in 1994, leading to a brief civil conflict.
The Southern Movement (Al-Hirak) formed in 2007 and demands greater autonomy or independence.
Houthi insurgency began after Hussein al-Houthi, the movement's founder, was killed in Saada in 2004.
Houthis captured Sanaa in 2014, forcing President Hadi to flee abroad in 2015.
In 2017 the Houthis claimed a missile attack on Riyadh's King Khalid International Airport.

subtopics.title: India-UAE partnership
subtopics.summary: India and the UAE agreed to double bilateral trade to over USD 200 billion by 2032. Their ties span energy, with a long-term LNG deal, civil nuclear cooperation and defence collaboration, along with a proposal for data embassies. The UAE also accounted for 18% of India's remittance flows.
facts: India and the UAE agreed to double bilateral trade to over USD 200 billion by 2032.
Bilateral trade was US$ 100 billion in FY 2024-25.
The UAE is India's 3rd largest trade partner, after China and the US.
In 2022, India became the first country with which the UAE signed a CEPA.
ADNOC Gas signed an agreement with HPCL to supply 0.5 million tonnes per annum of LNG for 10 years.
The UAE accounted for 18% of India's remittance flows.
India has access to the UAE's Al Dhafra Air Base for refuelling.
Both countries agreed to explore cooperation in small modular reactors and nuclear safety.
A proposal for offshore digital infrastructure would store critical national data as data embassies.

subtopics.title: UAE profile and the Kafala system
subtopics.summary: The UAE is a federal elective monarchy of seven emirates, with Abu Dhabi as its capital and the dirham as its currency. Under the Kafala system, an in-country sponsor, typically the employer, controls a migrant worker's visa and legal status. Workers cannot change jobs or leave the country without that sponsor's permission.
facts: The UAE is a federal elective monarchy composed of 7 emirates.
The UAE shares land borders with Oman and Saudi Arabia.
The UAE's maritime borders in the Persian Gulf are with Qatar and Iran.
The UAE's capital is Abu Dhabi and its currency is the dirham.
Mohammed bin Zayed Al Nahyan is the President; Mohammed bin Rashid Al Maktoum is the Prime Minister.
Kafala means 'sponsorship' in Arabic.
Under Kafala, an in-country sponsor, typically the employer, controls a worker's visa and legal status.
Workers cannot change jobs or leave the country without the sponsor's permission.
Kafala can lead to exploitation, non-payment of wages, poor conditions and restricted movement.
Barakah is the Arab world's first nuclear power plant.

subtopics.title: Republic Day 2026 Parade and Chronology
subtopics.summary: Republic Day celebrations begin on 23 January, observed as Parakram Divas, and conclude on 29 January with the Beating Retreat Ceremony at Vijay Chowk. The main events fall on 26 January, when the Prime Minister pays homage at the Amar Jawan Jyoti and the President unfurls the National Flag at Kartavya Path. The 2026 parade, the 77th Republic Day, showcased Constitutional values through 30 cultural tableaux.
facts: Festivities officially begin on 23 January, observed as Parakram Divas.
23 January marks the birth anniversary of Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose.
The President delivers the Republic Day Address on the day before Republic Day.
The Prime Minister pays homage at Amar Jawan Jyoti in early morning of 26 January.
The President unfurls the National Flag at Kartavya Path (formerly Rajpath).
The National Anthem and a 21-gun salute follow the flag unfurling and mark the formal start of the parade.
The President confers Padma and Gallantry Awards in the evening of 26 January.
Celebrations conclude on 29 January at Vijay Chowk with the Beating Retreat Ceremony.
2026 is India's 77th Republic Day; the theme is 150 Years of Vande Mataram.
Top tableaux: Maharashtra, Jammu & Kashmir and Kerala; Chief Guests: Ursula von der Leyen and Antonio Costa.

subtopics.title: Padma and Gallantry Awards
subtopics.summary: Padma Awards are announced every year on the eve of Republic Day and recognise achievements in all fields involving public service. Gallantry Awards honour bravery of armed forces personnel and are announced twice a year. The Padma Awards 2026 conferred 131 honours, and Shubhanshu Shukla received the Ashok Chakra.
facts: Padma Awards 2026 conferred 131 honours in total.
The 2026 Padma list included 5 Padma Vibhushan, 13 Padma Bhushan and 113 Padma Shri.
Padma Awards were instituted in 1954 and are announced annually on the eve of Republic Day.
Padma categories in order of rank: Padma Vibhushan, then Padma Bhushan, then Padma Shri.
Gallantry Awards were conferred on 70 Armed Forces personnel.
Shubhanshu Shukla, the first Indian on the ISS, was honoured with the Ashok Chakra.
Ashok Chakra is India's highest peacetime gallantry award.
Gallantry Awards are announced twice a year, on Republic Day and Independence Day.
Wartime Gallantry was instituted on 26 January 1950; Peacetime Gallantry in 1952.
Gallantry eligibility covers officers of all ranks (Army, Navy, IAF), reserve forces, Territorial Army and nursing services.

subtopics.title: History of Republic Day
subtopics.summary: 26 January was linked to the Poorna Swaraj declaration from the Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress in December 1929. From 1930 to 1947 the day was celebrated as Independence Day or Poorna Swaraj Day. The Constitution, adopted on 26 November 1949, came into effect on 26 January 1950, making India a sovereign democratic republic.
facts: The Lahore Session of INC in December 1929 passed the Poorna Swaraj resolution.
Poorna Swaraj called for total self-rule, sovereignty and complete independence from British rule.
The Declaration of Independence was officially promulgated on 26 January 1930.
From 1930 to 1947, 26 January was celebrated as Independence Day or Poorna Swaraj Day.
The Constitution was adopted by the Constituent Assembly on 26 November 1949.
The Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950.
The Constitution repealed the Indian Independence Act 1947 and the Government of India Act 1935.
India ceased to be a Dominion of the British Crown and became a Sovereign, Democratic Republic.
India gained independence on 15 August 1947.
26 November has been observed as Constitution Day since 2015.

subtopics.title: Unfurling and Hoisting the Flag
subtopics.summary: On Republic Day the President unfurls the Tricolour, while on Independence Day the Prime Minister hoists it. The difference reflects the two events: unfurling renews commitment to Constitutional principles, and hoisting symbolises the rise of a new nation.
facts: On 26 January the President of India, as Head of State, unfurls the Tricolour.
On 15 August the Prime Minister, who heads the Union Government, hoists the National Flag.
On 26 January the flag is folded or rolled and attached to the top of a pole.
The President unveils the flag without pulling it up.
On 15 August the flag is positioned at the bottom of the pole and raised from bottom to top.
Unfurling is a symbolic gesture to renew commitment to the principles of the Constitution.
Unfurling highlights India's shift from a British colony to a Sovereign, Democratic Republic.
Hoisting symbolises the rise of a new nation, patriotism and freedom from colonial rule.

topics.title: UGC (Promotion of Equity in Higher Education Institutions) Regulations, 2026

subtopics.title: University Grants Commission: Origin, Status and Functions
subtopics.summary: The University Grants Commission is a statutory body under the UGC Act, 1956, formally inaugurated in 1953 by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad. Its idea evolved from the Sargeant Report (1944), and the University Education Commission (1948) recommended restructuring it on the British model. The UGC allocates grants, advises the government on higher education reforms and maintains academic standards from its headquarters in New Delhi.
facts: Statutory body under the UGC Act, 1956
Formally inaugurated in 1953 by Maulana Abul Kalam Azad
Idea evolved from the Sargeant Report (1944)
University Grants Committee set up in 1945, expanded by 1947 to oversee all Indian universities
University Education Commission (1948) chaired by Dr. S. Radhakrishnan
That Commission recommended restructuring UGC on the British model
In 1952, the government entrusted UGC with oversight of higher education grants
Functions: allocating grants, advising government, maintaining academic standards
Composition: Chairman, Vice-Chairman and 10 members appointed by Central Government
Headquarters: New Delhi

subtopics.title: Caste Discrimination and Legal Safeguards
subtopics.summary: UGC data show that caste-discrimination complaints rose by 118 per cent between 2019-20 and 2023-24, and pending cases grew sharply despite high disposal rates. Caste discrimination erodes equality, dignity and fraternity and limits SC, ST and OBC access to elite institutions. Constitutional articles and statutes such as the Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955 and the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989 provide the legal safeguards.
facts: Caste-discrimination complaints rose 118%, from 173 (2019-20) to 378 (2023-24)
Pending caste-discrimination cases rose from 18 to 108 over the same period, despite high disposal rates
Rohith Vemula (2016) and Payal Tadvi (2019) cases spotlight alleged institutional caste exclusion
Caste discrimination erodes equality, dignity and fraternity
Caste bias and poor schooling limit SC/ST/OBC access to elite institutions
Marginalised groups face higher dropout rates due to academic, financial and psychological pressures
SC/ST cells in universities often lack autonomy and enforcement
Article 14: equality before law; Article 15: prohibits discrimination and allows affirmative action; Article 17: abolishes untouchability
Protection of Civil Rights Act, 1955; SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, 1989; Right to Education Act, 2009

subtopics.title: Key Provisions of the 2026 Regulations
subtopics.summary: The 2026 Regulations define caste-based discrimination broadly, covering direct, indirect and systemic discrimination, and aim to prevent discrimination on campuses. Equal Opportunity Centres, which are mandatory in all higher education institutions, house Equity Committees that must act on complaints within set timelines. Institutions face reporting duties, and non-compliance can lead to penalties such as debarment from UGC schemes.
facts: Caste-based discrimination is defined to include unfair or biased treatment
Covers direct, indirect and systemic discrimination
Prevents discrimination on campuses based on caste, religion, gender, race, disability or place of birth
Equal Opportunity Centres: nodal body, mandatory in all higher education institutions
Equity Committee: Head as Chairperson; 3 senior faculty, 1 non-teaching staff, 2 civil society and 2 student representatives; EOC coordinator as Member Secretary
Equity Committee convenes within 24 hours of a complaint; inquiry report due within 15 working days
Ombudsperson: independent authority for appeals against unresolved equity grievances; decisions binding on institutions
EOCs submit bi-annual reports; institutions submit annual equity compliance reports; National Monitoring Committee meets at least twice a year
Non-compliance can lead to debarment from UGC schemes, restrictions on offering degrees, or withdrawal of UGC recognition

subtopics.title: Concerns Raised About the Regulations
subtopics.summary: Critics fear the framework could indirectly influence the social and demographic composition of campuses. They point to the absence of safeguards against false or malicious complaints and to the lack of confidentiality or timely redress for the accused. Short inquiry periods and the automatic linkage of the helpline to police are also seen as risks.
facts: Demographic policing concerns: may indirectly influence the social and demographic composition of campuses
No explicit protection against false, frivolous or malicious complaints
No mechanisms for confidentiality or timely redress for the accused; risk of reputational damage
Compressed inquiry timelines may compromise fact-finding and increase the risk of errors
Helpline's automatic linkage to police may discourage open academic discourse and reporting
Students and faculty could fear criminal consequences

subtopics.title: Launch, Aim and Management
subtopics.summary: The Startup India Initiative was launched on 16 January 2016 to foster startup culture and build an inclusive ecosystem for innovation and entrepreneurship. The Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade, under the Ministry of Commerce & Industry, manages it. 16 January is observed as National Startup Day, and India marks 10 years of the initiative.
facts: Launched on 16 January 2016.
Aim: foster startup culture and build an inclusive ecosystem for innovation and entrepreneurship.
Managed by the Department for Promotion of Industry and Internal Trade (DPIIT), Ministry of Commerce & Industry.
16 January is observed as National Startup Day.
India ranks as the world's third largest startup hub, after the US and China.
Soonicorn: a startup with potential to reach a valuation of 1 billion dollars in the near future.
Decacorn: valuation of 10 billion dollars.
Hectocorn: valuation of 100 billion dollars.

subtopics.title: Eligibility and Core Features
subtopics.summary: A startup qualifies if it is headquartered in India, opened less than 10 years ago and has an annual turnover below 100 crore. The initiative offers ease of doing business through self-certification and single-window clearances. Eligible startups also enjoy tax exemptions for three consecutive financial years.
facts: A startup must be an entity headquartered in India.
It must have opened less than 10 years ago.
Annual turnover must be less than 100 crore.
Ease of doing business through simplified compliance, self-certification and single-window clearances.
Eligible startups enjoy tax exemptions for 3 consecutive financial years.
Sector-specific policies target biotechnology, agriculture and renewable energy.
Funding support includes a 10,000 crore Fund of Funds for early-stage funding.

subtopics.title: Funding Support Schemes
subtopics.summary: Startup India funding support works through the Seed Fund Scheme, the Credit Guarantee Scheme and the Fund of Funds for Startups. The Fund of Funds was introduced in June 2016 with a corpus of 10,000 crore to enhance access to domestic capital. Seed assistance covers early activities such as proof of concept and market entry, delivered through eligible incubators.
facts: Seed Fund Scheme provides financial assistance for proof of concept, prototype development, product trials, market entry and commercialization.
Seed Fund assistance is delivered through eligible incubators.
Credit Guarantee Scheme offers credit guarantees for loans to DPIIT-recognized startups.
Fund of Funds for Startups was introduced in June 2016.
Fund of Funds corpus is 10,000 crore.
Fund of Funds aims to enhance access to domestic capital.
Fund of Funds supports early-stage funding.

subtopics.title: Incubation and Innovation Schemes
subtopics.summary: Several schemes support startups through incubation, technology focus and regional reach. Atal Incubation Centres, set up under the Atal Innovation Mission of NITI Aayog, provide physical infrastructure. TIDE 2.0, GENESIS, NIDHI and ASPIRE target emerging technologies, Tier-II and Tier-III cities, technology-driven ideas and agro-industry respectively.
facts: Atal Innovation Mission operates under NITI Aayog.
Atal Innovation Mission establishes Atal Incubation Centres that provide physical infrastructure and support to startups.
TIDE 2.0 stands for Technology Incubation and Development of Entrepreneurs.
TIDE 2.0 supports startups in emerging technologies such as AI, IoT and Blockchain.
GENESIS 2024 stands for Gen-Next Support for Innovative Startups.
GENESIS aims to boost startups in Tier-II and Tier-III cities.
NIDHI stands for National Initiative for Developing and Harnessing Innovations.
NIDHI aims at socio-economic growth through wealth and job creation.
ASPIRE stands for A Scheme for Promotion of Innovation, Rural Industries and Entrepreneurship.
ASPIRE sets up a network of technology centres and incubation centres and promotes startups in agro-industry.

subtopics.title: Mentorship, Networking and Events
subtopics.summary: BHASKAR connects startups, investors and mentors to empower non-metro cities, while MAARG offers intelligent matchmaking between mentors and startups. Startup Mahakumbh is a flagship event bringing together startups, unicorns, soonicorns, investors, industry leaders and ecosystem stakeholders. The fifth edition is scheduled in March in New Delhi.
facts: BHASKAR stands for Bharat Startup Knowledge Access Registry; it is the BHASKAR Platform of 2024.
BHASKAR connects startups, investors and mentors.
BHASKAR aims to empower non-metro cities.
MAARG stands for Mentorship, Advisory, Assistance, Resilience & Growth.
MAARG offers intelligent matchmaking between mentors and startups.
Startup Mahakumbh is a flagship event bringing together startups, unicorns, soonicorns, investors, industry leaders and ecosystem stakeholders.
The 5th Startup Mahakumbh is scheduled in March in New Delhi.

subtopics.title: Deal Background and Significance
subtopics.summary: India and the EU concluded the India-EU Broad-based Trade and Investment Agreement, finalised at the 16th India-EU Summit in New Delhi. The deal closes nearly two decades of intermittent negotiations and is widely described as the 'Mother of All Deals'. It still awaits ratification by the Indian Parliament and European bodies before full implementation.
facts: Concluded by PM Modi and EU President Ursula von der Leyen
Finalised at the 16th India-EU Summit, New Delhi
Makes the EU India's 22nd Free Trade Agreement partner
Officially the Broad-based Trade and Investment Agreement (BTIA)
Negotiations began in 2007, suspended in 2013, revived in 2022
Supports India's trade diversification and China-plus-one strategy
Counters rising global trade protectionism, especially from the US
Creates an economic space for two billion people

subtopics.title: Tariff Cuts and Market Access
subtopics.summary: Duties on over 90% of bilateral trade have been removed under the agreement. The EU will eliminate customs duties on 99.5% of Indian exports, while India will phase out tariffs on over 90% of EU goods. High-value sectors such as cars and wines are opened gradually through staged tariff cuts and quotas.
facts: Duties on over 90% of bilateral trade removed
EU eliminates customs duties on 99.5% of Indian exports
Estimated $33 billion boost to labour-intensive sectors
Textiles and apparel, leather and footwear, gems and jewellery enter EU at 0% duty
India phases out tariffs on over 90% of EU goods
Machinery up to 44%, chemicals up to 22%, pharmaceuticals up to 11%
EU exporters to save approximately EUR 4 billion annually
Luxury car tariff (cars above EUR 15,000) falls from 110% to 10% in 5 years
Tariff rate quota of 250,000 cars per year
Premium wine tariffs fall from 150% to 20-30%; spirits to 40%

subtopics.title: Protections, Exclusions and CBAM
subtopics.summary: Both sides keep negative lists of sensitive farm goods to protect rural livelihoods and food security. A parallel agreement protects geographical indications such as Darjeeling Tea and Champagne. The EU's Carbon Border Adjustment Mechanism applies a carbon levy on selected imports from 1 January 2026, and India received a most-favoured-nation assurance on it without a full exemption.
facts: India's exclusions: dairy, wheat, rice and poultry
EU's exclusions: beef, sugar and rice
Geographical indication protection for Darjeeling Tea and Champagne
EUR 500 million pledged for decarbonisation of Indian industries
CBAM full implementation with carbon levy from 1 January 2026
Transitional phase 2023-2025 involved reporting only, with no financial levy
CBAM sectors: cement, aluminium, fertilisers, iron and steel, hydrogen, electricity
CBAM certificate price linked to the EU ETS carbon price
Credit allowed if a carbon tax was already paid in the exporting country
India got an MFN assurance on CBAM but no full exemption

subtopics.title: 2030 Roadmap and the US Factor
subtopics.summary: The 'Towards 2030' Joint India-EU Comprehensive Strategic Agenda is a five-year framework adopted at the 16th Summit to move ties beyond trade. It is organised into pillars covering prosperity, technology, security, connectivity, and enablers such as skills and mobility. The deal is also framed as a hedge against US tariff policy, after 50% reciprocal tariffs on Indian goods were imposed in August 2025.
facts: Official title: 'Towards 2030: Joint India-EU Comprehensive Strategic Agenda'
A five-year framework adopted at the 16th India-EU Summit
Prosperity and Sustainability pillar includes green hydrogen and carbon market alignment
Technology and Innovation pillar includes Trade and Technology Council and 6G, semiconductors, quantum
Security and Defence pillar focuses on maritime security in the Indo-Pacific
Connectivity pillar includes IMEC and the EU's Global Gateway initiative
Enablers pillar covers skills and mobility, with a European Legal Gateway in India
Mutual recognition of professional qualifications targeted by 2030
50% reciprocal tariffs on Indian goods imposed in August 2025
Described as creating a 'Third Pole' in global trade

subtopics.title: EU Basics and India-EU Ties
subtopics.summary: The European Union is a political and economic union of 27 member states, and it traces its origins to the European Coal and Steel Community formed in 1951 by six countries. Its key institutions include the Commission, Parliament, Council, Court of Justice and the European Central Bank. India and the EU have had diplomatic relations since 1962, and ties were upgraded to a Strategic Partnership in 2004.
facts: EU is a political and economic union of 27 member states
Began as the European Coal and Steel Community (1951) with six founding members
European Commission: executive body that proposes laws and manages the budget
European Parliament: the EU's only elected legislative body
European Council: heads of state or government, sets political direction
Court of Justice of the EU ensures uniform application of EU law
Diplomatic relations with the European Economic Community established in 1962
Upgraded to a Strategic Partnership at The Hague Summit in 2004
EU is India's largest trading partner in goods and largest foreign investor
Bilateral trade in 2024-25 was $136.53 billion

subtopics.title: Demographic Winter: Meaning and Key Indicators
subtopics.summary: Demographic winter is a persistent and structural decline in population growth, and it is no longer limited to developed countries. Its key indicators are fertility below the replacement level of 2.1 and an inverted population pyramid with a rising old-age dependency ratio. It can lead to a shrinking workforce, a rising fiscal burden from ageing and a potential loss of the demographic dividend.
facts: Demographic winter: a persistent and structural decline in population growth.
Now a global phenomenon, not limited to developed countries.
Fertility rate below replacement level of 2.1 children per woman.
Inverted population pyramid: shrinking young population and expanding elderly population.
Rising old-age dependency ratio is a key indicator.
Demographic dividend: growth potential from a larger working-age population compared to dependents.
Total fertility rate (TFR) is the average births per woman; 2.1 is the replacement level.
Fertility refers to children born to a woman during reproductive years (ages 15-49).

subtopics.title: Causes and Negative Impacts of Demographic Winter
subtopics.summary: Causes include delayed life milestones, urbanisation, societal and cultural shifts, and greater access to family planning. A declining population brings a shrinking workforce, pressure on pension and healthcare systems, and greater isolation of the elderly. Developed nation trends suggest that a rebound is unlikely once fertility falls below the replacement level.
facts: Delayed milestones: later marriages and parenthood due to career priorities, economic insecurity and high housing and education costs.
Urbanisation: smaller and costlier urban housing discourages larger families.
Societal shifts: greater female workforce participation, preference for smaller families and changing family norms.
Access to family planning gives greater reproductive autonomy and reduces unintended births.
Shrinking workforce threatens future labour supply as youth replacement falls short over time.
Ageing population raises the burden on healthcare, elderly care and pension systems.
Low-fertility states face youth shortages; high-fertility states struggle with overpopulation.
Smaller families disrupt traditional support systems, leading to greater elderly isolation.
Declining fertility and late marriages are linked to social isolation and mental health challenges.
Developed nation trends show that a rebound is unlikely once rates fall below replacement level.

subtopics.title: China's Birth Control Policy: Timeline
subtopics.summary: China's approach moved from birth control being a minor priority under Mao Zedong to a central policy push in the 1970s. The One-Child Policy (1980) restricted most couples to a single child, and it was later replaced by a Two-Child Policy and a Three-Child Policy (2021). Fertility rates did not rebound despite these relaxations.
facts: Pre-1970s (Mao Zedong era): birth control existed but was not a major policy priority.
Great Leap Forward (1958-62) aimed to boost production and living standards but resulted in famine and millions of deaths.
Population growth rebounded after the Great Leap Forward was rolled back.
1970s five-year plans promoted birth control, often through coercive measures.
Slogan 'Later, Longer, Fewer' encouraged delayed marriages, longer intervals between births and fewer children.
One-Child Policy (1980) formally restricted most couples to a single child.
The One-Child Policy aimed to curb rapid population growth and ease pressure on resources.
Three-Child Policy introduced in 2021.
Fertility rates have not rebounded despite the relaxations.

subtopics.title: Reasons for China's Population Decline
subtopics.summary: China's total fertility rate fell to 1.3 births per woman in the 2020 Census, far below the replacement level of 2.1. The One-Child Policy is credited with cutting the TFR from 2.75 in 1979, but fertility did not rebound after later relaxations. Female education, changing family norms, economic pressures and the COVID-19 pandemic are cited as further causes.
facts: TFR declined to 1.3 births per woman (2020 Census), far below the replacement level of 2.1.
The One-Child Policy is credited with reducing TFR from 2.75 (1979) to 1.3 (2020).
Fertility did not rebound after the Two-Child (2016) and Three-Child (2021) relaxations.
The lack of rebound indicates deep-rooted behavioural and socio-economic shifts.
Higher female education and employment have enhanced women's autonomy over reproductive decisions.
Growing disengagement from traditional family structures has reduced pressure to marry early or have many children.
Intense job competition, high urban living costs and work-life imbalance discourage marriage and childbearing.
Housing pressures and economic uncertainty discourage fertility, especially among younger generations.
COVID-19 related mortality and economic uncertainty further accelerated the population decline.
Delayed childbirth and smaller family sizes follow from higher education and employment of women.

subtopics.title: Global and Indian Fertility Context
subtopics.summary: UNFPA's State of World Population 2025 reports a global TFR of 2.25 in 2024, projected to reach the replacement level by 2050. India's fertility rate in 2025 was 1.9, below replacement, with wide regional differences. National schemes such as the National Population Policy 2000, ASHA workers and Janani Suraksha Yojana focus on voluntary choice, institutional deliveries and maternal and child health.
facts: UNFPA was founded in 1969 as the United Nations Fund for Population Activities and renamed in 1987.
Global TFR was 2.25 in 2024 and is projected to hit replacement level of 2.1 by 2050.
Highest TFR: Niger > Somalia > DR Congo; lowest TFR: South Korea < Hong Kong < Singapore.
Elderly (65+) share of population: Japan 30%, Europe 20%, India 7%.
India's fertility rate in 2025 was 1.9, below the replacement level of 2.1.
India's working-age population (15-64 years) is 68%.
Above-replacement states: Bihar (2.98) > Meghalaya > UP > Jharkhand > Manipur.
National Population Policy 2000 aimed at replacement-level fertility (TFR 2.1) through voluntary choice.
Janani Suraksha Yojana encourages institutional deliveries and provides free delivery, transport and postnatal care.
Proposal to raise the legal age of marriage for girls to 21 years under the Prohibition of Child Marriage Act 2006.

topics.title: UN High Seas Treaty Enters Into Force

subtopics.title: BBNJ Agreement: scope and objectives
subtopics.summary: The UN High Seas Treaty, also called the BBNJ Agreement, is a legally binding treaty for ocean spaces beyond national jurisdiction. It was negotiated under a UN-led intergovernmental conference and aims to safeguard biodiversity in these areas. It contributes to the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework, which targets 30% protection of land and sea by 2030.
facts: Also called UN High Seas Treaty; adopted in 2023.
Legally binding international treaty governing ocean spaces beyond national jurisdiction.
Covers the high seas and the International Seabed Area.
These areas are global commons, open to all states for navigation, overflight, submarine cables and pipelines.
Third implementing agreement under UNCLOS, alongside the 1994 Part XI Agreement and the 1995 UN Fish Stocks Agreement.
Core objective: safeguard biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction.
Contributes to the Kunming-Montreal Global Biodiversity Framework.
Four pillars: Marine Genetic Resources, Area-Based Management Tools, Environmental Impact Assessments, Capacity Building and Technology Transfer.
Conference of the Parties (COP) is the decision-making body.
Ratified by 83 countries; India has signed, ratification pending.

subtopics.title: UNCLOS and maritime zones
subtopics.summary: The 1982 UN Convention on the Law of the Sea (UNCLOS) sets the legal framework for all activities in the oceans and seas and is called the constitution for the oceans. It divides ocean space into zones with different levels of state control, from full sovereignty in the territorial sea to free navigation on the high seas. It also created three international institutions.
facts: UNCLOS (1982) is also called the constitution for the oceans.
It has 168 parties and sets out the legal framework for all activities in the oceans and seas.
The Convention created three new institutions at the international level.
International Tribunal for the Law of the Sea: independent judicial body for disputes on interpretation or application of the Convention.
International Seabed Authority: ensures protection of the marine environment from harmful effects of deep-seabed activities.
Commission on the Limits of the Continental Shelf: facilitates establishing outer limits of the continental shelf beyond 200 NM from baselines.
Territorial sea: the state has full sovereignty.
Exclusive Economic Zone: extends to 200 NM; the state has the right to exploit all economic resources.
High seas: free for navigation by vessels of all nations.
1 NM (nautical mile) = 1.852 km.

subtopics.title: Fisheries sector in India and its schemes
subtopics.summary: India's fisheries sector contributes 7.43% to agriculture gross value added, the highest among agriculture and allied sectors. India ranks high globally as a producer, aquaculture producer and exporter. Government schemes such as Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana aim to modernise the sector and support fish farmers and micro and small enterprises.
facts: Total fish output (2024-25): 197.75 lakh tonnes.
Fisheries contribute 7.43% to agriculture GVA, the highest among agriculture and allied sectors.
India is the 2nd largest producer (8% of world production) and 2nd largest aquaculture producer.
India is the 4th largest exporter; the United States is the largest importer of Indian seafood.
Pradhan Mantri Matsya Sampada Yojana was introduced in 2020 under the Atma Nirbhar Bharat Package.
Matsya Sampada investment: Rs 20,050 crore.
National Fisheries Development Board, established 2006, works under the Ministry of Fisheries, Animal Husbandry and Dairying.
PM Matsya Kisan Samridhi Sah-Yojana: sub-scheme for fisheries micro and small enterprises, investment Rs 6,000 crore.
Implementation period of the Sah-Yojana: 2023-24 to 2026-27.
India's first riverine dolphin estimation counted 6,327 dolphins across 28 rivers in 8 states.

subtopics.title: WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies
subtopics.summary: The WTO Agreement on Fisheries Subsidies was adopted at the 12th Ministerial Conference in 2022 and entered into force in September 2025. It aims to set binding rules to curb harmful fisheries subsidies, especially those linked to illegal fishing. India did not join the agreement, citing the need to protect small fishers, livelihoods and food security.
facts: Adopted at the 12th Ministerial Conference, 2022.
Entered into force in September 2025, after approval by two-thirds of members.
Objective: establish binding rules to curb harmful fisheries subsidies.
Prohibited: subsidies linked to Illegal, Unreported and Unregulated (IUU) fishing.
Prohibited: subsidies for fishing on overfished stocks.
Prohibited: support for fishing in unregulated high seas.
Members must submit fisheries-related data.
Supports SDG 14: conserve and sustainably use oceans, seas and marine resources.
India did not join, citing the need to protect small fishers, livelihoods and food security.
WTO Fish Fund provides aid to developing and LDC members for implementation.

subtopics.title: PSLV-C62 failure and its cause
subtopics.summary: ISRO's first launch of 2026, PSLV-C62, was scheduled from Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh. A third-stage solid rocket anomaly disrupted high-thrust delivery to the upper stages, which affected the intended satellite orbital injection. The failure came 8 months after the PSLV-C61 setback.
facts: Mission was ISRO's first launch of 2026
Scheduled liftoff from Sriharikota, Andhra Pradesh
Fault: 3rd-stage solid rocket anomaly
Effect: high-thrust delivery to upper stages disrupted
Impact: intended satellite orbital injection affected
Failure came 8 months after the PSLV-C61 setback

subtopics.title: PSLV rocket profile and history
subtopics.summary: The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle is called the Workhorse of ISRO and is a four-stage medium-lift launcher, first launched in 1993. It uses solid propellants in its first and third stages and liquid propellants in its second (Vikas engine) and fourth stages. It can carry up to 1750 kg to a 600 km Sun-synchronous orbit.
facts: Nickname: Workhorse of ISRO
Type: four-stage medium-lift launch vehicle
Launched in 1993; first success in 1994 with IRS-P2
Stages 1 and 3 use solid propellants
Stages 2 (Vikas engine) and 4 use liquid propellants
First Indian launch vehicle equipped with liquid stages
Payload: up to 1750 kg to a 600 km Sun-synchronous orbit
Record: 104 satellites in one launch (2017)
Notable missions: Chandrayaan-1, Mars Orbiter Mission, Aditya-L1, AstroSat

subtopics.title: PSLV-C62 payloads
subtopics.summary: PSLV-C62 carried EOS-N1 (Anvesha), a hyperspectral imaging satellite developed for DRDO's Strategic Applications, and KID, a small re-entry prototype from a Spanish startup. It also carried AayulSAT, India's first on-orbit satellite refuelling payload. In total, 18 co-passenger satellites flew on the mission.
facts: EOS-N1 (Anvesha): hyperspectral imaging satellite
EOS-N1 developed for DRDO's Strategic Applications
EOS-N1 intended orbit: Sun-synchronous orbit

AayulSAT developed by Bengaluru-based OrbitAID Aerospace
18 co-passenger satellites (domestic and international)
Commercial payloads from India, Mauritius, Luxembourg, UAE, Singapore, Europe and the US

subtopics.title: ISRO launch vehicles, private players and policy
subtopics.summary: India's launch vehicle family ranges from the early SLV and GSLV to the planned NGLV, which has a maximum payload capability of 30 tonnes. The SSLV serves small satellites and takes that load off the PSLV. Private firms such as Agnikul Cosmos are building their own rockets, which the Indian Space Policy 2023 allows.
facts: SLV: ISRO's first satellite launch vehicle, followed by ASLV

topics.title: National Sports Governance Act and India's Sports Framework

subtopics.title: National Sports Board and Election Panel
subtopics.summary: The National Sports Board is the apex regulatory body for sports governance in India and can grant, renew, suspend or cancel recognition of national sports bodies. Its members are selected and appointed by a Search-cum-Selection Committee chaired by the Cabinet Secretary. A National Sports Election Panel, drawn from experienced former election officials, oversees elections in sports federations.

Board accounts are audited by the Comptroller and Auditor-General of India

subtopics.title: Rules 2026 and National Sports Bodies

The National Olympic Committee and National Paralympic Committee are the sole governing bodies for Olympic and Paralympic sports in India. Recognised sports bodies are deemed public authorities under the RTI Act 2005.

Executive Committee must include at least 4 women members

National Paralympic Committee is the sole governing body for Paralympic sports
Other bodies include National Sports Federations and Regional Sports Federations
Term of members: 3 years or up to 65 years of age, whichever is earlier
A person convicted by a court and sentenced to imprisonment is disqualified
Recognised sports bodies are deemed public authorities under the RTI Act 2005

subtopics.title: National Sports Tribunal
subtopics.summary: The National Sports Tribunal is set up for independent, speedy, effective and cost-efficient resolution of sports disputes. It is headed by a sitting or retired Supreme Court judge or a High Court Chief Justice, with two other members. Its jurisdiction covers election disputes, athlete selection issues and governance matters, but excludes major international events and doping-related disputes.

subtopics.title: Anti-Doping Framework
subtopics.summary: Anti-doping in India is handled by the National Anti-Doping Agency, set up under the Ministry of Youth Affairs & Sports, and by the National Anti-Doping Act, 2022. National Anti-Doping Agency monitors doping control programmes

subtopics.title: Sports Initiatives and Performance
subtopics.summary: Government initiatives include Fit India, Khelo India, KIRTI and TOPS, which aim at fitness participation, talent identification and support for Olympic medal prospects. KIRTI (2024) aims to identify talent among school children aged 9 to 18

subtopics.title: UN Security Council and Control Regimes
subtopics.summary: The UN Security Council is one of the six principal organs of the United Nations, established in 1945 under the UN Charter, and it has five permanent and ten non-permanent members. Its main purpose is maintaining international peace and security. Outside the Council, the Australia Group and the export control regimes NSG, MTCR and Wassenaar Arrangement work to limit the spread of dangerous weapons.

subtopics.title: Critical Technology and Mineral Security
subtopics.summary: Pax Silica is a US-led framework to build trusted technology supply chains, covering semiconductors, AI infrastructure, critical minerals and advanced manufacturing, and India is set to join it. India's National Critical Minerals Mission and KABIL aim to secure critical mineral assets at home and abroad.

quizzes.title: Strike and Legal Debate
quizzes.passage: United States forces carried out a military strike on Venezuela, known as Operation Absolute Resolve. The strike targeted Caracas, Miranda, Aragua and La Guaira, and it led to the capture of Venezuelan President Nicolas Maduro. The action has raised a legal question: can a law enforcement objective justify the use of military force on a sovereign territory? Arguments in favour cite the claim that fentanyl and narco-gangs cause mass American deaths. Opponents warn that crime can become an excuse to violate borders. Some sections of Venezuela's domestic opposition have endorsed stronger external pressure, which indirectly supports Washington's interventionist stance. Venezuela says the intervention reflects geopolitical interests rather than genuine concern over migration or narcotics control.

Its proposed mandate includes supervising and guiding the civil administration of Gaza and its security and stabilisation force, mobilising international financial and technical assistance, and ensuring transparency, coordination and accountability during Gaza's transition from conflict to reconstruction. Beyond Gaza, the Board is being presented as a possible template for managing complex global conflicts. Its approach marks a move away from traditional universal multilateral institutions. quizzes.title: Chagos Dispute Check
quizzes.passage: The Chagos Islands have been at the centre of a long dispute between Britain and Mauritius. Before Mauritius became independent, Britain set up the islands as a separate territory, and they stayed under British control after independence. In that period, native Chagossians were forcibly removed from their homes so that a military base could be built on Diego Garcia, the largest island in the archipelago. Mauritius responded through international legal channels. It took the matter to the Permanent Court of Arbitration in The Hague, which found that Britain had violated Mauritius' rights under a major international maritime convention. Britain, however, insisted that the issue should remain a bilateral matter between the two countries. Mauritius then turned to the United Nations, where the General Assembly voted on a resolution seeking an advisory opinion from the International Court of Justice. quizzes.title: Republic Day Chronology and History
quizzes.passage: India celebrates Republic Day on 26 January every year to honour the adoption of its Constitution in 1950, which established a sovereign democratic republic. The festivities officially begin on 23 January, observed as Parakram Divas in honour of Netaji Subhash Chandra Bose's birth anniversary. On the day before Republic Day, the President of India delivers the Republic Day Address to the nation. Early on 26 January, the Prime Minister pays homage at the Amar Jawan Jyoti. The President then unfurls the National Flag at Kartavya Path, formerly known as Rajpath, followed by the National Anthem and a 21-gun salute that marks the formal start of the parade. In the evening, the President confers the Padma and Gallantry Awards. The celebrations conclude on 29 January at Vijay Chowk with the Beating Retreat Ceremony. The history of the day goes back to the Lahore Session of the Indian National Congress in December 1929, which passed the Poorna Swaraj resolution calling for complete independence from British rule. From 1930 to 1947, 26 January was celebrated as Independence Day or Poorna Swaraj Day. India gained independence on 15 August 1947, which led to a re-evaluation of the significance of Republic Day. The Constitution came into effect on 26 January 1950, ending India's status as a Dominion of the British Crown.

quizzes.title: Caste Discrimination and Safeguards
quizzes.passage: Caste-based discrimination in higher education has drawn sustained national attention. Figures reported by the University Grants Commission show that complaints of caste discrimination rose sharply in recent years, and the number of pending cases also grew, even though disposal rates stayed high. Two high-profile cases have highlighted allegations of institutional caste exclusion across the country. Such discrimination is seen to erode equality, dignity and fraternity, and to undermine trust in democratic institutions. Caste bias and poor schooling limit access to elite institutions for SC, ST and OBC students, which hinders social mobility. Marginalised communities also face higher dropout rates because of academic, financial and psychological pressures, while reserved category stigma can produce anxiety, low self-esteem and poor academic outcomes. Support structures are not always effective either, since SC/ST cells in universities often lack autonomy and enforcement, weakening grievance redressal. The constitutional framework responds to these problems. Article 14 guarantees equality before law, Article 15 prohibits discrimination and permits affirmative action, and Article 17 abolishes untouchability. Several statutes add enforcement, including the Protection of Civil Rights Act, which imposes penalties for practising untouchability, the SC/ST (Prevention of Atrocities) Act, which sets strict punishments, and the Right to Education Act, which promotes non-discriminatory access to education. Together, these measures combine constitutional principles with statutory penalties and guarantees of access to education.

quizzes.passage:
India and the European Union have concluded a free trade agreement that is widely described as a landmark in their economic relationship. The deal was finalised at the 16th India-EU Summit held in New Delhi, and it is expected to create an economic space covering around two billion people. It brings to a close a long series of talks that began in 2007, were suspended for a period, and were later revived. The agreement is also a response to a changing global trade environment. quizzes.title: Birth Control Policy in China
quizzes.passage: China's approach to family size has changed several times since the Mao era. In the early phase, birth control existed under Mao Zedong, but it was not a major policy priority. Later, the government's five-year plans began promoting birth control, and in some cases the measures used were coercive. A strict limit on family size was then introduced, and this limit was relaxed in stages over the following decades. The relaxation did not bring fertility back to earlier levels. Women now have higher education and employment, which has enhanced their autonomy over reproductive decisions and contributed to delayed childbirth. Changing social attitudes, economic pressures and high urban living costs and housing pressures are also among the factors linked to the trend. Many young people delay marriage and childbirth because of job competition and work-life stress. Economic and social barriers also prevent many couples from having the number of children they desire. Smaller families, in turn, can disrupt traditional support systems for the elderly. The COVID-19 pandemic further accelerated the decline. Overall, the experience shows how policy changes alone may not reverse deep-rooted behavioural patterns in a population.

quizzes.title: Global and Indian Fertility Context

quizzes.title: BBNJ and the law of the seas
quizzes.passage: The world's oceans are divided into zones with very different legal status. Near a coast, a state has full sovereignty over its territorial sea, and its exclusive economic zone gives it the right to exploit economic resources. Further out lie spaces that belong to no single country. These spaces, known as areas beyond national jurisdiction, cover the high seas and the international seabed area. They are described as global commons and are open to all states for activities such as navigation, overflight and the laying of submarine cables and pipelines. Taken together, these areas make up a large share of the world's ocean surface, so their governance is a serious concern. The main legal framework for all ocean activities is the 1982 United Nations Convention on the Law of the Sea, often called the constitution for the oceans. Within that framework, a newer treaty was negotiated to protect biodiversity in areas beyond national jurisdiction. Its negotiations took place under a United Nations conference devoted to marine biodiversity in these areas. The new treaty is significant because it is the first global legal framework of its kind for protecting ocean biodiversity beyond national jurisdiction. It sits alongside the 1994 agreement on deep seabed mining and the 1995 UN Fish Stocks Agreement as part of the Convention's framework. Its goals also support wider global commitments on nature conservation, so it is closely tied to international biodiversity efforts.

quizzes.title: UNCLOS and ocean zones
quizzes.passage: The law of the sea rests on a simple idea: the closer a space lies to the coast, the greater a state's control over it. A state has full sovereignty over its territorial sea. Beyond that lies a zone in which the state holds the right to exploit all economic resources. Further still lie the high seas, where vessels of every nation may sail freely. The 1982 Convention on the Law of the Sea sets out the legal framework within which all activities in the oceans and seas must be carried out. It is often described as a constitution for the oceans. The Convention also created new institutions at the international level. One of these is a judicial body that settles disputes about how the Convention is interpreted. Another protects the marine environment from harmful effects of deep-seabed activities. A further body facilitates the establishment of the outer edge of the continental shelf. Continental shelf rights can extend beyond the basic zone limits, which makes the outer edge of the shelf a matter of legal importance. The Convention provides a process for determining that edge, and the bodies it created apply its rules in practice. The Convention is also supported by implementing agreements on particular issues, such as deep seabed mining and the management of fish stocks. Taken together, these rules form many layers of law that govern the oceans, and all users of the seas rely on this shared framework.

quizzes.title: PSLV-C62 mission check

ISRO planned its first launch of 2026 with PSLV-C62, a rocket scheduled to lift off from Sriharikota in Andhra Pradesh. The Polar Satellite Launch Vehicle is often called the workhorse of ISRO, and this flight carried a mix of government and commercial satellites. During the mission, a fault appeared in the third stage. A solid rocket anomaly disrupted the high-thrust delivery to the upper stages, and this affected the planned injection of the satellites into orbit. The failure came after an earlier setback with PSLV-C61, which put the vehicle under close scrutiny.

Among the payloads was EOS-N1, also known as Anvesha, an Earth observation satellite built for strategic applications. Another payload was KID, a small re-entry prototype developed by a Spanish startup, which was meant to splash down in the ocean. quizzes.title: UN and Control Regimes Check
quizzes.passage: The United Nations Security Council is one of the six principal organs of the United Nations and was established in 1945 under the UN Charter. Its main purpose is maintaining international peace and security. It addresses countries that threaten global security, authorises peacekeeping missions and imposes sanctions. In cases of international conflict, it can also authorise the use of force. The Council has fifteen members. Five of them are permanent members: China, France, Russia, the United States and the United Kingdom. The other ten are non-permanent members, and the General Assembly elects five of them each year for a two-year term. These ten seats are distributed on a regional basis. The Council's headquarters are in New York City. Several arrangements outside the Council work to limit the spread of dangerous weapons. The Australia Group was founded in 1985 in response to the use of chemical weapons during the Iran-Iraq War, and it works to prevent the proliferation of chemical and biological weapons. Three export control regimes also operate in this field: the Nuclear Suppliers Group, the Missile Technology Control Regime and the Wassenaar Arrangement. Each of these bodies is a separate arrangement with its own membership and purpose. The booklet presents these as part of the wider international effort against weapons proliferation.

questions.q:

quizzes.title: Economy and Rankings Check
quizzes.passage: India has climbed several global economic rankings in recent years. It overtook Japan to become the fourth-largest economy measured by nominal GDP, and it is projected to move ahead of another major economy to take third place. Its growth is described as the fastest among major economies, supported by strong domestic demand and a services-led model. Services form the largest share of the economy, followed by industry and agriculture. Food prices also entered a phase of deflation, meaning a sustained fall in the general price level. The Reserve Bank of India reported that states' consolidated fiscal deficit rose to 3.3 per cent of GDP in 2024-25. Rankings also measure other aspects of national standing. The Henley Passport Index ranks passports by the number of destinations that holders can reach without a prior visa, whether visa-free or on arrival. It was first launched in 2006 and is published by a London-based firm. NITI Aayog's Export Preparedness Index, now in its fourth edition, assesses how ready Indian states and union territories are to export. It is organised around four pillars: export infrastructure, business ecosystem, policy and governance, and export performance. The index supports India's goal of reaching one trillion dollars in merchandise exports by 2030.
